sentences.text: Hatzegopteryx is an extinct genus of azhdarchid pterosaur known from incomplete remains found in Transylvania, Romania.
The biggest known bones suggest a wingspan ranging from 10 to 12 meters, ranking it among the largest flying reptiles.
Its head was widened at the rear, reaching a width of 0.5 meters across the quadrate bones.
This creature possessed a sturdy skull that expanded backward and featured a massive lower jaw.
A medium-sized shoulder bone found in the Sânpetru Formation likely belonged to an individual with a wingspan of 4.5 to 5 meters.
The rear neck vertebrae could support loads between five and ten times the animal's own body weight.
The genus was formally named by Buffetaut and colleagues in the year 2002.
The authors responsible for the name were Buffetaut, Grigorescu, and Csiki.
The initial fossils were uncovered in the upper section of the Densuș Ciula Formation at Vălioara, Romania, dating to the Late Maastrichtian about 66 million years ago.
The type specimen, cataloged as FGGUB R 1083A, includes two pieces of the rear skull and a broken upper part of the left wing bone.
A single large neck bone known as the RR specimen or EME 215 was discovered at the Râpa Roșie site within the Sebeș Formation.
Scientists calculated the animal's size by comparing a 236-millimeter long wing bone fragment to those of Quetzalcoatlus.
Despite having a very large and strong skull, the animal was not flightless because its wing bones match those of other flying pterosaurs.
It was probably a terrestrial generalist predator, behaving like other azhdarchid pterosaurs.
Evidence points to this animal hunting prey that lived on the ground.
Its strong body structure implies it could kill animals too large to swallow whole, unlike other giant azhdarchids.
The robust anatomy suggests it may have targeted prey larger than other members of its family.
To hold up its heavy head, the neck likely contained very powerful muscles.
Researchers propose it functioned as the top predator in the Hațeg Island ecosystem because of its massive size.
Without large theropods present, this pterosaur was likely the apex predator of Hațeg Island during the Late Cretaceous, hunting prey proportionally larger than other azhdarchids.
It is suggested that this species played the role of the apex predator in the Hațeg Island ecosystem.
The generic name comes from the Hatzeg basin in Transylvania and the Greek word pteryx, which means wing.
The specific name thambema is taken from the Greek word thambema, meaning terror or monster, referencing its huge size.
A phylogenetic analysis conducted in 2018 placed Hatzegopteryx in an advanced position within the family Azhdarchidae.
The parent group for this genus is Azhdarchidae.
This animal lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Its time range corresponds to the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It inhabited the Tisia–Dacia Block, an island landmass that included the Hațeg Basin.
The island environment enjoyed a subtropical climate with an average temperature of about 25°C.
It is debated whether the RR specimen belongs to Hatzegopteryx thambema due to a lack of overlapping elements, though its bone structure warrants referral to at least H. sp.
It is debated whether similarities between Hatzegopteryx and Quetzalcoatlus northropi indicate synonymy, as the humerus is considered non-diagnostic for giant azhdarchids.

In their 2002 description, Buffetaut and colleagues suggested the skull weight must have been reduced in an unconventional way to allow flight, though they admitted it could have been a non-flying animal, finding this unlikely due to similarities in wing bones with flying pterosaurs.
Although initially identified as a third cervical vertebra, a set of traits supports its identification as a vertebra from the posterior neck, specifically the seventh vertebra.
